extracted.intended_audience: scientists, philosophers of science, and researchers interested in methods of scientific inquiry
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for assessing and selecting appropriate methods (deductive, empirical/experimental, observational) for studying complex phenomena and for constructing reliable scientific inferences. Emphasizes prerequisites, limitations, and verification for each method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of causation should be stated as tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: All laws of causation, in consequence of their liability to be counteracted, require to be stated in words affirmative of tendencies only, and not of actual results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use terminology that denotes tendency rather than asserting actual result (example: 'pressure' in mechanics = tendency to motion). Avoid phrasing laws as absolute results; recognize that what is called an 'exception' is often another concurrent law. Explain or re-categorize so-called exceptions as other causes acting concurrently (balloon/atmosphere example).

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize plurality of causes when generalizing from instances
rubrics_metrics.description: When an effect results from the union of many causes (Plurality of Causes), the share which each has is generally small, and the effect will not reliably follow any single cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not generalize from simple collations of instances when many causes concur. Expect instances where a candidate cause is present but effect absent, and vice versa, because other influences vary. Thus simple observation (method of agreement) will largely fail in such cases; quantitative differences may be of only secondary value.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of the Method of Simple Observation
rubrics_metrics.description: If the method merely collates instances of the effect, it is a method of pure observation; this is inapplicable to complex cases where many causes concur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pure observation can at best give vague general impressions and is almost never sufficient for intricate subjects (e.g., medical recovery, social phenomena). It requires either near-universal administration of the agent or that the effect be overwhelmingly dominated by one cause to be useful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirements and limitations of the Empirical/Experimental Method
rubrics_metrics.description: The empirical method operates upon the causes, trying different combinations of them to find which combination produces the given total effect; but it must be completely empirical (abstract from deductive knowledge) to be a true experiment on the complex case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Precautions usually required in experiments: (a) introduce the agent in circumstances exactly ascertained; (b) ensure no known circumstance has effects confoundable with those of the agent; (c) exclude other causes or make them such that their influence can be computed/allowed for. These are often unattainable in physiological, social, and historical cases. Multiplication of experiments may attenuate unknown causes but cannot fully overcome intermixture of influences. Some strong 'specifics' (quinine, etc.) may be established experimentally because of their large effect size.

rubrics_metrics.name: When experiments are chimerical for complex phenomena
rubrics_metrics.description: In phenomena so complicated it is questionable if two cases, similar in all respects but one, ever occurred; hence the experimental Method of Difference by comparing distinct cases is often chimerical.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be skeptical of arguments that equate collation of social/political instances with controlled experiment. Where causes are innumerable and changing, even artificially introducing a cause (e.g., a law) generally cannot be treated as a clean experiment because other influencing circumstances change before induction is possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Three essential components of the Deductive Method
rubrics_metrics.description: The Deductive Method consists of three operations: the first, one of direct induction (to learn laws of separate causes); the second, of ratiocination (reasoning/calculation from those laws); the third, of verification (comparing deductions with observation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Induction supplies the premises (laws of individual causes) which may themselves be obtained by observation, experiment, or deduction from simpler laws. Ratiocination can use mathematics/geometry where applicable. Verification is indispensable: deductions must be checked against direct observation wherever possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inductive prerequisite: ascertain laws of separate causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The first requisite of the Deductive Method is to know the laws of those tendencies; the law of each of the concurrent causes must be ascertained by previous observation or experiment (or by deduction from premises ultimately grounded in observation).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study each tendency where it operates alone or only with agencies whose effects are calculable. Avoid attempting to infer a tendency's law from cases where it is counteracted or heavily intermixed. Use the fourfold method of experimental inquiry (discussed earlier) and, where possible, apply Method of Concomitant Variations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental selection for physiological investigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Physiology is hampered because separating agencies often destroys the phenomena; pathological facts (diseases) can serve as valuable equivalents to experimentation by producing localized disturbances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer experiments in conditions where circumstances are ascertained (often health, not disease). Observe early stages of pathological disturbances if using disease as an experimental probe. Artificial interventions (e.g., nerve section, mercury administration) can be used to discover general laws when chosen so that secondary cascading effects are minimized or can be accounted for.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ratiocination: calculation from laws of causes
rubrics_metrics.description: The second stage is determining from the laws of the causes what effect any given combination will produce — a process of calculation (ratiocination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When precise numerical laws exist, mathematical/theoretical tools (calculus, geometry) may be required; but in many complex cases numerical/analytical calculation is intractable. Ratiocination may still determine directional or qualitative expectations (what antecedent conditions produce a given effect) without full numerical precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verification as a decisive test
rubrics_metrics.description: To warrant reliance on general conclusions arrived at by deduction, these conclusions must be found, on careful comparison, to accord with the results of direct observation wherever it can be had.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If known cases exist in which the deduced effect does not follow, one must explain what frustrated it; absent such explanations the theory is imperfect. Verification converts deduction from conjecture into trustworthy knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Experimental design precautions for studying causes
rubrics_metrics.description: When devising an experiment to ascertain the effect of a given agent, introduce the agent into circumstances exactly ascertained and exclude or account for other causes whose effects could be confounded with those of the agent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If unknown influencing circumstances exist, they may disguise the agent's effect. Use control of known confounders or make them calculable. When separation is impossible, use multiplicity of experiments across varied circumstances to make it improbable that unknown causes are the same in all trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate method depends on the nature of the phenomenon
rubrics_metrics.description: Two of the three methods (pure observation and direct experiment) are in many complex cases inefficient or illusory; often only the deductive (a priori) method remains practicable for complex phenomena.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select method according to the complexity and plurality of causes: for simple or strongly specific causes, direct experiment may suffice; for highly composite phenomena (politics, history, many social effects), rely on deduction from well-established laws of the separate causes and strict verification.
